title: Cloud Computing
topics: AI and Big Data in Cloud

bullets.text: Overview of lecture topics: meaning, features, models, advantages, challenges, applications.
Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services over the internet.
Services include servers, storage, databases, networking, software, and AI.
It's a way of renting computing resources instead of buying and maintaining them.
Analogy: paying for electricity without owning the power plant.
On-demand self-service: users access resources without human interaction.
Broad network access: services available over the internet from various devices.
Resource pooling: providers share resources across multiple customers securely.
Rapid elasticity: resources can scale up or down quickly based on demand.
Measured service: usage is monitored and billed according to resources consumed.
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): delivers fundamental computing resources (e.g., virtual machines, storage).
Users build and manage their own applications on top of this infrastructure (e.g., AWS EC2).
Platform as a Service (PaaS): provides infrastructure plus a development platform.
Developers use built-in tools and frameworks without managing servers (e.g., Google App Engine).
Software as a Service (SaaS): delivers ready-to-use applications over the internet.
Users access software through a browser without installation (e.g., Gmail, Microsoft 365).
Public Cloud: services delivered over the internet, shared by multiple organizations.
Private Cloud: dedicated to a single organization, offering more control and security.
Hybrid Cloud: combines public and private clouds to balance flexibility with security.
Community Cloud: shared by several organizations with common goals (e.g., healthcare, education).
Reduced costs: less investment in hardware, maintenance, or data centers.
Improved scalability: easily expand or reduce resources during peak times.
Enhanced flexibility: access applications and data from anywhere with internet.
Reliability: leading providers offer backup, disaster recovery, and high availability.
Supports innovation: faster deployment and experimentation without infrastructure limits.

sections.heading: Challenges and Concerns in Cloud Computing

bullets.text: Security and privacy: trusting providers to protect sensitive information on remote servers.
Downtime: internet connectivity dependence can affect access to critical resources.
Compliance: adherence to strict regulations for data storage in certain industries.
Vendor lock-in: difficulty and cost in switching between cloud providers.
Performance concerns: issues with applications requiring very high processing speed or low latency.
Data storage and backup (e.g., Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive).
Business collaboration tools (e.g., Slack, Microsoft Teams).
Entertainment streaming platforms (e.g., Netflix, Spotify).
Healthcare solutions (e.g., electronic medical records, telemedicine, AI diagnosis).
Education platforms (e.g., Coursera, Google Classroom).
Research: large-scale data analysis, machine learning, and AI projects.
Growing use in AI and big data analytics, leveraging high-performance computing.
Edge computing: processing data closer to the source for reduced latency and real-time decisions.
Multi-cloud strategies: using services from multiple providers to avoid vendor lock-in.
Serverless computing: developers focus on code, with infrastructure managed by the provider.
Continued focus on security, compliance, and integration with AI, blockchain, and 5G.
